source.title: SAEmnesia: Erasing Concepts in Diffusion Models with Supervised Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: E. Cassano; Riccardo Renzulli; Marco Nurisso; Mirko Zaffaroni; A. Perotti; Marco Grangetto

page_placements.theme: Fixed-size fragmentation and duplication: one concept spread over several latents of one SAE

record.tranche_reason: The study compares unsupervised and supervised SAE training and reports that supervision concentrates concept scores into selected latents, refining the claim that feature splitting can depend on the SAE training objective. It does not test dictionary-size scaling.
record.gate_note: The study measures feature-score distributions, single-latent versus all-latent classification, and activation visualizations. It does not vary dictionary size, measure direction proximity between larger and smaller dictionaries, or test whether child features partition a parent's inputs. Unlearning benchmark and attack results are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper uses 'feature splitting' loosely, meaning a concept is spread over many latents of one unsupervised SAE, as motivation for its own supervised SAE. It then reports how well that method concentrates concepts and erases them. It never varies dictionary size or compares SAEs of different sizes. It does not test hierarchy, absorption or decomposition. On V6, it does not show that splitting comes from the sparsity objective acting on correlated inputs. It adds a supervised loss built to force each labeled concept onto one assigned latent, then shows that latent dominates the concept score. That deliberately induces the outcome rather than measuring splitting arising or shrinking under an alternative unsupervised objective such as Matryoshka.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that supervised concept labeling prevents feature splitting, as they define it (one concept spread over many latents), and binds each concept to one latent. They claim this yields more efficient and accurate single-latent concept erasure on UnlearnCanvas, in sequential unlearning, under attacks and for nudity. They also note that within-group interference remains, and that nudity needed two latents.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a supervised TopK SAE objective with concept-assignment and decorrelation losses, compared with the unsupervised SAE baseline; it does not test increasing dictionary sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature-score distributions and single-latent classification are compared across unsupervised and supervised SAE training; the k-NN result is described across denoising timesteps.

fits_no_version.finding: In an unsupervised TopK SAE (SD v1.5, block up.1.1), concept scores are low and dispersed across latents. A supervised concept-assignment loss yields one dominant latent per labeled concept (e.g. Flowers max 0.0166 vs 0.0404).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding supervised concept-latent assignment to an SAE concentrates a labeled concept's score into one latent, where an unsupervised SAE of the same size spreads it across many.

fits_no_version.finding: For nudity, SAeUron needed 205 top-scoring latents steered versus 2 for SAEmnesia-top2. Cats and Dogs share a most-active latent at 10 timesteps in SAeUron, and at 0–14 timesteps in the supervised variants depending on variant.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unsupervised SAEs on diffusion activations distribute single concepts across many latents, and latents are shared between similar concepts.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The evidence does not test dictionary-size scaling or geometrical/input-partition relations. Several feature comparisons are figure-based and give no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No other directly relevant feature-splitting measurement was omitted. The additional unlearning benchmark, sequential removal, and attack results measure erasure performance rather than feature splitting.

untested.parts: No dictionary-size sweep, coarse-to-fine replacement, input coverage or direction proximity.
There is no splitting measurement in large models or open SAE releases. The SDXL Turbo appendix reports only unlearning accuracy.
No nested families, geometric closeness or concept hierarchy.
No parent/child latent firing, absorption, or size/sparsity manipulation.
No cross-size latent decomposition or novel-latent analysis.

No test that splitting arises from the sparsity objective on correlated or hierarchical inputs, and no comparison with Matryoshka or other unsupervised objectives. The supervised loss forces concentration by design.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' label is removed. The concentration is the explicit training target of the supervised loss, so it is an induced outcome, not evidence about the sparsity objective's role in splitting. Rows R1–R4 and R8–R9 are own-method-versus-baseline comparisons, and R5–R7 validate the study's own method. The paper's 'feature splitting' differs from the dictionary-size sense in V1–V5.

versions.untested_parts: No dictionary-size sweep or test of coarse-to-fine feature replacement, input coverage, or directional proximity.
The preliminary SDXL Turbo experiment evaluates unlearning, not splitting at scale or across open SAE releases.
No test of nested feature families, their geometric closeness, or correspondence to a concept hierarchy.
No parent-child firing, absorption, or test of changing SAE size or sparsity to fix absorption.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents or analysis of novel latents and canonical units.

Tests supervised concept-assignment training against an unsupervised SAE, but not correlated or hierarchical inputs as the cause, Matryoshka SAEs, or whether the findings say little about the diffusion model's own units.

relation.reason: It uses the splitting notion as motivation and tests only its own method. The reader's 'tests' is not supported.

tranche.reason: The paper uses 'feature splitting' loosely, as motivation, and reports only how its own supervised SAE performs. It never varies dictionary size, so T4 fits. The reader's T5 is not supported.

source_check.notes: Here 'splitting' means one concept spread over many latents of a single SAE, not coarse-to-fine splitting as dictionary size grows. No version is tested and no verdicts apply. R2 values come from figure labels. The nudity results use SD v1.4, not SD v1.5.

statements.correction: Flowers max score: SAeUron 0.0166, SAEmnesia 0.0404 (SD v1.5, up.1.1). Nudity (SD v1.4, I2P, NudeNet): SAeUron steers 205 latents, 18 detections; SAEmnesia-TOP-2 steers 2, 9 detections; base SAEmnesia 47 detections.
statements.problem: None. Flowers 0.0166 (SAeUron) vs 0.0404 (SAEmnesia, neuron 11979) and 205 vs 2 latents (A.14) match. Context: the nudity result is on SD v1.4 (I2P), not SD v1.5, and base one-latent SAEmnesia did worse (47 vs 18 detections).
